name: Kira Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a charge-up unit underground at a big zinc mine. After the jumbo drills the face, I drive in, feed the explosive hose into each hole and wire it up for the blast at the end of shift. I've been there about eighteen months. Before that I was eight years on the phones at an insurance call centre, until they replaced most of us with a chatbot, so I'm not exactly new to this conversation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the work is real, you can see what you did, and the crew is a laugh. What wears me out is being the junior who has to double-check everything twice because I'm still learning the patterns. And money, always money: my husband Omar does bookkeeping from home part-time, and with Zara and Adam and the mortgage we're never more than a couple of weeks ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, it's a tool, not a takeover. I'd probably post a funny one about my old call centre chatbot that kept telling customers to restart their car. People at work would want me to say more, because they know I use the stuff every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing much changes, and that's fine. I use AI daily for little things: checking blast pattern questions before I ask the shift boss, pricing bikes for my weekend side thing, helping Zara with homework. If it plateaus there, I'm happy, it's useful and I'm in charge of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd push to get my ticket on the jumbo drill next year, which pays more. And I'd keep the weekend bike business going, fixing up second-hand bikes and selling them online, because that's about two hundred a month we really need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit relieved for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the bike business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It started when Adam outgrew his bike and I fixed it up to sell. Now I buy wrecks at the recycling centre, fix them in the garage, and the AI helps me write the ads and guess the price. It's not much, but it's mine, and it paid for the school camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relieved for everyone else. Not for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already got the shock once, at the call centre. I was angry for about a week and then I went looking. I think once it's happened to you, you stop being scared of it in the same way.

S0.say: She'd say AI is a tool, not a takeover, and post a joke about her old call centre's chatbot. Workmates would expect her opinion because she uses it daily.
S0.think: She thinks little changes for her and that suits her. She uses AI daily for work questions, her side business and her daughter's homework, and feels in charge of it.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims for her jumbo drill ticket next year for better pay. Keeps her weekend business fixing and selling second-hand bikes, worth about two hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm, and a bit relieved for others.
S0.quote: I was angry for about a week and then I went looking.
S0.fieldNote: Kira has already lost a job to AI and come out the other side, which shapes her calm. She uses AI as a practical tool across work, family and a small side business. Her thin cushion is real, but she has more than one income stream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, don't wait. I'd tell the crew it's not the end of the world, I've seen a job disappear and people found other things. But I'd also say the company should give fair notice and training, that's only reasonable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the charge-up work gets automated in a few years, there are already robot charging arms being tested at other mines. That doesn't scare me too much, I'd move to something next to it. What worries me more is Omar, because bookkeeping is exactly the kind of thing the AI eats first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the trial crew for any new charging robot, so I'm the one who knows how it works. I'd help Omar learn the new AI accounting tools so he can take on more clients instead of fewer. And I'd grow the bike business a little, maybe add repairs for the neighbours, so there's more coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Omar. For me it's almost interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Omar feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's quieter about this stuff than me. He's good with numbers and terrible with change, the opposite of me. When the call centre went, he was the one who couldn't sleep, and I was the one making a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be on the trial crew. Isn't that training the thing that replaces you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But someone's going to train it, and the person who trains it is the last one they let go. At the call centre the girls who helped set up the chatbot got moved to complaints, and the rest of us got letters.

S1.say: She'd tell people to get ready rather than wait, and that it's not the end of the world. She'd also say the company should give fair notice and training.
S1.think: She thinks charge-up work will be automated within a few years but she can move to related work. She worries more about Omar, since bookkeeping is the kind of work AI takes first.
S1.do: Volunteers for the trial crew on any new charging robot and helps Omar learn AI accounting tools to take on more clients. Expands the bike business with repairs for neighbours.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on Omar's behalf; for herself it's almost interesting.
S1.quote: At the call centre the girls who helped set up the chatbot got moved to complaints, and the rest of us got letters.
S1.fieldNote: Kira's adaptability turns her worry towards her partner, whose work is more exposed to thinking AI. Her strategy of training the machine that replaces her is drawn directly from what she saw at the call centre. She takes a pragmatic view rather than blaming anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's different, this isn't a call centre, it's everything at once, and the government needs to catch people. I'd say it plainly at work. Even I'm not going to pretend there's a quick fix for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and robots doing hands-on work too, means the mine and Omar's clients and probably my bike repairs all go at once. I can adapt, but adapt to what? When the call centre went, there was a mine down the road hiring. This time there's no mine down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Omar and cut everything back to the mortgage, food and power. I'd still try to be in whatever jobs are left at the mine, the ones overseeing the robots, for as long as they last. And I'd sell the bike stock while people still have money to buy bikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time I've pictured it and not had a next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zara and Adam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zara's twelve and she asks the AI everything, so she'd know before I said anything. I'd tell her we're going to be fine because we're good at figuring things out. Adam would just want to know if he still gets his birthday bike, and I'd make sure he does, even if I build it from parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the government, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that pays the mortgage while people work out what's next, not forever, just to stop the panic. And honest information, what jobs will exist and where. I can move fast if I know which way to run.

S2.say: She'd say this is different from a call centre closing because it's everything at once, and the government needs to catch people. She wouldn't pretend there's a quick fix.
S2.think: She thinks the mine, Omar's clients and even her bike repairs would all go together. Unlike when the call centre closed, there'd be no nearby employer to move to.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the mortgage, food and power in the first week. Holds on to any remaining robot-supervision jobs at the mine and sells off her bike stock while people can still buy.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because for the first time she can't see a next step.
S2.quote: When the call centre went, there was a mine down the road hiring. This time there's no mine down the road.
S2.fieldNote: This is the one picture that breaks Kira's usual confidence, because her past recovery relied on another employer nearby. She stays practical and still plans, but admits she has no next step. She asks for income support and clear information, framed as temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, that's long enough to do something about it, so let's do it. I'd tell people at work to learn the new tools now. I'd also say the government should be setting up the safety net now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough for me to get into the robot side at the mine and maybe learn to maintain the charging units. It still ends badly for most jobs, but I'd want to be the last one turning the lights off, not the first one sent home. And it gives Omar time to find a new line of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the jumbo ticket in the first year and then put my hand up for any automation training going. I'd use the AI to map out courses and to study at night. Omar and I would try to save some of the bike money each month instead of spending it, so we have two or three months put by when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Omar retrain in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about it a bit. He's patient and careful, he'd be good at something with people, maybe a teacher's aide or working with older people. He'd hate the idea at first and then he'd be great at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd want to be the last to turn the lights off. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. Maybe by then there's a new kind of work, or a new kind of support. I'm good at the next step, not the five steps after it.

S3.say: She'd say five years is long enough to act, urge workmates to learn the new tools now and call for the government to build the safety net early.
S3.think: She thinks five years lets her move to the robot side of the mine and perhaps maintain charging units. Most jobs still go, but she'd aim to be among the last, and Omar would have time to change fields.
S3.do: Gets her jumbo ticket in the first year, then joins any automation training. Uses AI to plan and study, and saves part of the bike income each month to build two or three months of savings.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and being busy helps.
S3.quote: I'm good at the next step, not the five steps after it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Kira back the sense of having a next step. She is honest that she can't see far past it. Her planning for Omar shows how much of her energy goes into the household rather than just her own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time that it's on all of us to get ready. It's not a disaster if we use it. I'd tell people to stop arguing about whether it's coming and start working out what they'll do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, honestly, I think I'm fine. I'd move up into the robot side, maybe end up looking after the fleet, and the kids would be through school. If almost every job goes by 2036, then it's everybody's problem, and that's when big new deals get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the jumbo ticket, then the automation training, then maybe a maintenance certificate over the decade. I'd grow the bike business slowly and save from it, and help Omar move into care work over a few years. I'd keep using AI daily, getting better at it as it gets better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Curious about what it'll look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if it's everybody's problem, big deals get made. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when it's only call centre girls, nobody marches. When it's doctors and lawyers and miners all at once, the people in charge have to do something. I might be wrong, but that's my gut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money between now and then. We're one broken car away from trouble, every month. Ten years of good planning can still get knocked over by one bad winter.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough that it's on everyone to prepare, and urge people to stop arguing about whether it's coming and plan instead.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be fine over a decade, moving into the robot side and with her children through school. If nearly every job goes, it becomes everyone's problem, which she expects will force big new deals.
S4.do: Takes the jumbo ticket, then automation training and possibly a maintenance certificate over the decade. Grows the bike business slowly and saves from it, helps Omar move into care work, and keeps building her AI skills.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, and curious about what it will look like.
S4.quote: When it's doctors and lawyers and miners all at once, the people in charge have to do something.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Kira's calm returns, resting on her track record and a belief that a society-wide shock forces a response. She still names thin savings as the real weak point. Her plan mixes career steps, a side income and support for her partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because for once I couldn't see a next step, and Omar and I would both lose work together. What would help is something that covers the mortgage for a while and honest information about where the work will be. Give me a direction and I'll run.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask people what they learned the last time they lost a job. Most of us have been through something. That's worth more than any course.

headlineQuote: Give me a direction and I'll run.
portrait: Kira Usman is a 43-year-old charge-up operator at a large underground zinc mine, eighteen months in after losing a call centre job to a chatbot. She uses AI every day and runs a small weekend business fixing and selling second-hand bikes. Her husband Omar does part-time bookkeeping from home, a job she sees as more exposed than her own. She's calm in the slower pictures and treats change as a series of next steps, but the two-year AGI picture alarms her because it leaves no nearby employer to move to. With five or ten years she plans to move into the robot side of the mine and help Omar shift into care work.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she and Omar would both lose work at once and she couldn't see a next step.
whatWouldHelp: Temporary help covering the mortgage and honest information about where the work will be.
